query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, minor addition of niobium (≈2–3 at%) during alloy processing of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will lead to the in-situ formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich precipitates at the lamellar phase boundaries, thereby stabilizing the microstructure during thermal cycling and long-term mechanical loading and enhancing both room-temperature creep resistance and corrosion stability.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy produced with a uniform, fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that currently shows a promising strength–ductility balance but suffers from limited performance in long-term creep and corrosion environments under extreme temperature fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 2–3 atomic percent niobium during melting and casting.
generation.conditions: The Nb addition is incorporated during alloy processing (melting and casting) followed by standard thermo-mechanical treatments; the modified alloy is then evaluated under cyclic temperature conditions and long-term mechanical loading representative of aerospace fastener service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich precipitates that segregate at lamellar phase boundaries to pin interfaces and stabilize the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby reducing room-temperature creep. They also help maintain a more uniform and stable passive film, which enhances corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Nb-modified alloy is expected to exhibit improved creep resistance and enhanced corrosion stability under cyclic temperature fluctuations while maintaining the balanced strength and ductility required for aerospace applications.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy processed by current methods without any Nb addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only when the Nb content is maintained within ≈2–3 at% and the processing conditions ensure uniform Nb distribution; deviations in Nb levels or thermal treatment protocols may alter precipitate formation and compromise ductility.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary evidence supports improved creep and corrosion resistance with Nb additions in similar alloy systems, the precise magnitude of performance enhancement under prolonged service conditions remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: a control set without Nb and a test set with an added 2–3 at% Nb, processed under identical melting, casting, and thermo-mechanical conditions. Subject both sets to long-term creep tests under constant load at room temperature and accelerated temperature cycling, and perform corrosion tests in environments simulating chloride-containing acid exposures.
measurements: Creep rate and time-to-failure under controlled loading
Tensile yield strength and ductility after aging tests
Corrosion rate and passive film characteristics via electrochemical tests
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to verify the presence and uniformity of Nb-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in creep resistance (e.g., reduced creep rate or enhanced lifetime), show no evidence of coherent Nb-rich precipitates at phase boundaries, or fail to exhibit improved corrosion stability (as measured by corrosion current density and passive film quality) compared to the control, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). drafts.hypothesis: Minor addition of a micro‐alloying element (e.g., titanium) will promote the formation of coherent, finely dispersed precipitates at the lamellar interfaces of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing the alloy’s strength–ductility balance, its resistance to room-temperature creep, and its corrosion stability.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure produced at large sizes, currently possessing insufficient balance between strength and ductility, along with limited resistance to creep and corrosion.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor addition (approximately 1–3 wt%) of titanium during alloy processing.
drafts.conditions: Intervention is applied during melting and casting; subsequent standard thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., solution treatment and aging) is used. The improvement is evaluated under industrially relevant temperature cycles and mechanical loading conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent, nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates preferentially nucleated at the lamellar interfaces, which modify the phase boundary properties and enhance overall microstructural stability.
drafts.mechanism: Titanium acts as a nucleation agent for precipitates that provide dual benefits: (1) impeding dislocation motion by a precipitation-strengthening mechanism that improves yield strength while preserving ductility, and (2) stabilizing lamellar interfaces by retarding grain-boundary sliding and diffusive processes, thereby improving creep resistance and offering sites that enhance passivation for corrosion resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy is anticipated to show increased yield strength and improved ductility, lower room-temperature creep rates, and improved corrosion resistance relative to the starting material. The overall performance should better meet the requirements for aerospace fastener applications.
drafts.baseline: The performance characteristics (strength–ductility balance, creep rate, and corrosion resistance) of the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy produced via existing processing routes.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under industrial processing conditions with minor alloying additions not exceeding ∼3 wt% Ti. Effects may differ if Ti levels are too high or if thermal treatments substantially deviate from the established protocols.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set with no Ti addition (control) and another with a 1–3 wt% addition of Ti under otherwise identical processing conditions. Subject both sets to identical thermo-mechanical processing and then conduct a series of mechanical tests (tensile, creep at room temperature), corrosion tests in relevant aggressive environments, and microstructural analyses (using TEM/SEM) to detect the presence, size, and distribution of Ti-rich precipitates at lamellar interfaces.
measurements: Corrosion rate via potentiodynamic polarization tests
Microstructural characterization (size, distribution of precipitates; lamellar interface integrity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength and ductility (or show a deterioration), or if no coherent Ti-rich precipitates are observed at lamellar interfaces, or if the creep and corrosion resistance do not improve relative to the control, the hypothesis that minor Ti addition enhances practical performance via the proposed mechanism will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of a refractory element (e.g., tungsten) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will lead to the in situ formation of fine, coherent W-rich precipitates that improve strength, ductility, high-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar microstructure exhibiting a suboptimal strength–ductility balance and limited high-temperature performance.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small addition (around 1–2 wt%) of tungsten into the alloy’s composition during processing.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is processed under the same manufacturing conditions as the base alloy (e.g., casting and controlled cooling) with post-heat treatments tailored to promote coherent precipitate formation. Mechanical testing (tensile, creep, and corrosion tests) is carried out across ambient to elevated temperatures to simulate aerospace environment stresses.
drafts.structural_mediator: Fine, coherent tungsten-rich precipitates embedded within the eutectic matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The W-rich precipitates are expected to act as obstacles to dislocation motion (precipitation strengthening) while promoting microstructural stability by impeding grain boundary sliding and diffusion. This modifies dislocation dynamics and enhances high-temperature resistance, thereby improving both strength and ductility without compromising long-term creep and corrosion resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the tungsten-modified alloy should exhibit increased yield and ultimate tensile strengths with a maintained or improved ductility, as well as improved high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion behavior under simulated operational environments.
drafts.baseline: Data from the current AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy performance demonstrates a trade-off between strength and ductility, along with limited high-temperature (room-temperature creep) and corrosion resistance.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected only if the tungsten addition promotes uniform precipitate formation without causing deleterious phases or excessive brittleness; extreme deviations in processing conditions or tungsten concentrations outside a narrow optimum window may negate the benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with a 1–2 wt% tungsten addition. Process both sets under identical conditions, including the same heat-treatment protocol aimed at optimizing precipitate formation. Conduct a series of standardized tensile tests, high-temperature creep tests, and corrosion tests under simulated aerospace conditions.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength from tensile tests
Creep rate under a fixed load at elevated temperatures
Corrosion rate under controlled corrosive environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase in yield strength and ductility, along with a measurable reduction in creep and corrosion rates) compared to the baseline alloy under the test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Nb (≈2–3 at%) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates at the fcc/B2 interfaces. This modification is expected to pin grain boundaries and stabilize the lamellar microstructure during thermal cycling and long-term loading, thereby enhancing creep and corrosion resistance while maintaining the alloy’s balanced strength and ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 2–3 atomic percent Nb during alloy melting and casting.
drafts.conditions: Service environments characterized by extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep), and corrosive conditions relevant to aircraft and spacecraft fasteners.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates at phase boundaries and within the matrix that pin grain boundaries and hinder dislocation and interface motion.
drafts.mechanism: Nb addition is expected to drive the formation of stable nanoprecipitates that act as obstacles to grain boundary migration and dislocation motion. This results in reduced creep rates at elevated temperatures and a microstructure that resists coarsening under thermal cycling. In addition, the Nb-rich regions may help stabilize passive films on the alloy surface, thereby improving corrosion resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Nb-modified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 should exhibit lower high-temperature creep rates, enhanced phase stability under thermal cycling, and improved corrosion resistance, while retaining an excellent balance of strength and ductility.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, which already shows a favorable strength–ductility balance but falls short of industrial performance criteria in terms of long-term creep and corrosion resistance under extreme environmental conditions.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on maintaining a low Nb concentration (≈2–3 at%) to avoid the excessive formation of brittle phases. The modified processing route must also ensure a uniform Nb distribution and controlled nanoprecipitate size; deviations may negate the improvements or compromise ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens using identical casting and thermomechanical processing: one set with the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and one with an added 2–3 at% Nb. Subject both sets to accelerated aging tests at elevated temperatures, constant-load creep experiments, and standardized corrosion tests (e.g., salt spray and electrochemical assessments).
measurements: Tensile and creep tests at room and elevated temperatures to assess strength, ductility, and creep rate
Corrosion rate measurements using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and salt spray tests
Microstructural characterization via TEM and atom probe tomography to verify nanoprecipitate formation, distribution, and coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-containing alloy fails to show statistically significant improvements in creep resistance and corrosion stability compared to the baseline (or if it suffers an unacceptable loss in ductility or strength) under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Nb (approximately 2–3 atomic %) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its long‐term creep resistance and corrosion stability under extreme temperature fluctuations.
drafts.material_initial_state: The as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a fine, uniform lamellar microstructure (fcc/B2 or fcc/L12) that exhibits good room‐temperature strength and ductility but shows limitations in long‐term mechanical loading (creep) and corrosion resistance under temperature cycling.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a minor Nb addition (2–3 at.%) into the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is processed under similar casting and thermomechanical conditions as the original material, then subjected to long‐term mechanical (creep) testing and corrosion evaluation under cyclic temperature and corrosive (chloride-containing acid) environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nb is expected to segregate preferentially at the lamellar phase boundaries, forming fine Nb‐rich precipitates or modifying the interphase chemistry, which will stabilize the microstructure (by pinning interfaces and dislocations) and promote a more robust, protective passive film at the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: The Nb addition will increase high-temperature microstructural stability by inhibiting grain-boundary sliding and dislocation motion (thus reducing creep) while also improving corrosion resistance by enhancing the chemistry and adherence of the protective passivation layer.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Nb-modified alloy should exhibit a reduced creep rate and lower degradation in mechanical strength under long-term loading at elevated temperatures, along with lower corrosion current densities and more stable passive film characteristics compared to the Nb-free baseline.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without Nb addition, which has demonstrated excellent strength and ductility but limited creep and corrosion resistance in challenging service environments.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be most effective when the Nb content is carefully controlled (approximately 2–3 at.%) and when processing conditions allow uniform distribution of Nb at the phase boundaries; effects may vary if the Nb content is too high or if subsequent heat treatments alter the intended microstructural modifications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with an added 2–3 at.% Nb. Process both sets with identical casting and post-treatment protocols to obtain similar lamellar microstructures. Subject both sets to (a) long-term creep testing at elevated temperatures (e.g. 700°C) under a fixed load and (b) corrosion testing in a controlled chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution under cyclic temperature variations.
measurements: Creep rate and time-to-failure under constant load at elevated temperatures
Tensile yield and fracture strength after creep tests
Electrochemical parameters (e.g., corrosion current density, passivation behavior) from potentiodynamic polarization tests
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM/SEM analysis of Nb distribution and phase stability)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate (or an improvement in creep lifetime) and does not exhibit a measurable improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., no lower corrosion current density or enhanced passive film stability) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
